headline: Texas Gov.-elect Hinojosa backs a statewide vote on THC access
dek: Gina Hinojosa told The Texas Tribune on 18 November she would revoke Greg Abbott's under-21 hemp THC order and that Texans deserve an election on THC.
key_points: Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said in a Texas Tribune interview on 18 November that people deserve an election on access to THC.
She said she would revoke Governor Greg Abbott's executive order banning sales of hemp-derived THC products to people under 21.
She left the method to lawmakers: Texas has no citizen initiative, so any statewide vote has to be sent to the ballot by the Legislature.
Hinojosa takes office on 19 January 2027; legalization bills HB 362 and HB 369 are already filed for the session that starts in January.
body: The incoming governor of Texas has said, on the record, that voters should decide the question of THC access. In an interview with The Texas Tribune held on Wednesday 18 November, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, was asked whether she wanted the Legislature to address THC. Her answer was that people want access, that there should be an election, and that lawmakers would have to work out how.

In the same interview she said she would revoke Governor Greg Abbott's ban on selling hemp-derived THC products to people under 21. That ban was made by executive order, not by statute. Hinojosa takes office on 19 January 2027.
## What she said, and what she did not

The exchange was short. The Tribune's interviewer listed several Abbott executive orders and asked which she would rescind. On the under-21 hemp THC sales ban, the published transcript records that she would revoke it. Asked next about the Legislature, she said: "I think people deserve an election on that issue."

She did not say what the election would be about in legal terms. She did not say adult-use legalization, a regulated hemp market, or a constitutional amendment. She said the Legislature will have to tackle it the way it sees fit. That leaves a wide range of outcomes inside one sentence.

She also did not say what would replace the under-21 order. USA Today, which identified the order as Executive Order GA-56, noted that the Legislature never passed such a ban itself. Revoking the order without a replacement would remove the age rule that the order created. We flag that as an open question, not a prediction: the interview does not say whether she wants an age limit set by statute instead, and it does not say what happens to agency rules written while the order was in force.
> A governor can lift an order on day one. A statewide vote on THC needs the Legislature, and that is where this will be decided.
## Why a vote is hard to get in Texas

Texas does not let citizens put measures on the ballot by collecting signatures. A statewide vote has to come from the Legislature. The usual route is a proposed constitutional amendment, which needs a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate before it goes to voters, who then decide by simple majority. The governor has no formal role in that process.

So Hinojosa's statement is a signal of political support, not a mechanism. It matters because it removes the threat of a veto and tells lawmakers of her own party what she would welcome. It does not move a bill.

The Senate is the place to watch. The Texas Tribune reported on 18 November that advocates see the clearest path to adult-use legalization the state has had. Sarah Todd, director of the Texas Cannabis Policy Center, told the Tribune that some Republican senators support cannabis law reform, and that the mood of the new Senate is not yet known. As we reported on 13 November, Lieutenant Governor-elect Vikki Goodwin, who will preside over the Senate, has put THC regulation on her reserved list of 30 priority bills.
## The bills already on file

Lawmakers began filing bills on 9 November. As we reported on 10 November, House Democrats filed HB 362 and HB 369 to legalize adult-use cannabis, with home growing of up to 12 plants and a tax stack of 15% plus 20%. The Tribune describes the bills, filed by Representatives Joe Moody of El Paso and John Bucy of Austin, as allowing adults 21 and older to possess 2 ounces of cannabis, including up to 15 grams of concentrate.

Those are ordinary bills. They would legalize by statute, with no public vote. An election of the kind Hinojosa described would need a different vehicle, most likely a joint resolution. Whether sponsors now pair their bills with one is the first practical test of her comment.
## What it means for hemp sellers

Texas has no adult-use market. Its legal THC trade is almost entirely hemp. The Tribune reports that the Department of State Health Services lists about 14,000 retail locations licensed to sell consumable hemp, and that the industry generates around $300 million a year in state tax revenue. Advocates told the Tribune the sector's small businesses employ more than 50,000 people.

That market has been shrinking. The health department adopted rules this year enforcing a 0.3% total THC limit, which the Tribune says removes smokable hemp, more than half the inventory at some stores. The federal hemp ban due on 11 December would go further and outlaw nearly all consumable hemp products nationwide.

Hinojosa's promise touches only one piece of that: the age order. It does not undo the health department's total THC rules, and no governor can undo the federal definition. Lukas Gilkey, chief executive of the hemp manufacturer Hometown Hero, told the Tribune the industry will ask lawmakers to repeal the state rules. Todd said none of the early-filed legalization bills says how existing hemp businesses would be treated, and that her group has raised it with the sponsors.
## What it means for medical operators

The state's medical programme, the Texas Compassionate Use Program, is the only legal source of marijuana in Texas. Its licence holders have often been at odds with hemp sellers. Their response to the new political map is cautious. Nico Richardson, chief executive of Texas Original, told the Tribune that safety standards for all THC products and wider medical access should stay priorities in 2027. A spokesperson for goodblend said the company welcomes the adult-use debate and listed the questions that would need answers first: who tests products, what growing and manufacturing standards apply, and how the medical programme keeps working for patients.

For investors, the point is scale and sequence. Katharine Neill Harris of Rice University's Baker Institute told the Tribune that 24 other states have built full legal cannabis markets. Texas would be by far the largest state yet to join them. But nothing in this week's comments sets a date, and the route Hinojosa prefers, a public vote, is slower than a bill.
## What to watch

Watch 19 January 2027, when Hinojosa takes office and can act on executive orders. Watch whether a joint resolution for a statewide THC vote is filed alongside HB 362 and HB 369 once the session opens in January. Watch the Senate: committee assignments under Goodwin, and whether any Republican senator signs on, will show if two-thirds is in reach. And watch 11 December, when the federal hemp ban is due to take effect and Texas's 14,000 hemp retail locations learn how much of their stock remains legal under federal law.
